name: Daria Farah

opening.speaker: interviewer
opening.text: I’m with the independent Work Futures Panel. We have no ties to AI companies, employers, unions, political parties or government, and we don’t sell anything or campaign. What you tell me is confidential. Could you walk me through a normal working day?

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: I’m Daria Farah, 27, and I lead a line crew for an electricity company. I check the switching plan, make sure everyone has the right gear, and then we go out to repair or replace lines; I’m usually the one who decides if the weather makes a job unsafe.

opening.speaker: interviewer
opening.text: What do you most value in the work, and what is the hardest part?

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: I like seeing a crew bring a dark street back on, and I take pride in having learned the trade properly. A long cold call-out is tiring, but the harder thing is that my pay has not left much room to save; I have less than one month of expenses set aside.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: AI Plateau: Picture this. AI turns out to be mostly hype. It automates some routine tasks and saves a bit of time here and there, but nothing radical changes. Jobs, pay and prices carry on much as they would have anyway.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I’d say a small program can make the job sheet neater, but it cannot tell from the road whether a line is swaying too much. The crew still has to go and look before anyone touches the equipment.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I don’t expect this little change to take my job, since most of my day is outside with the crew. I do worry about money already, and a slow month would make me ask my sister for help.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I’d let the office try the job-sheet program, but I’d check the details before using them in a safety briefing. I’d keep the call-out rota and bring lunch from home more often so I can put a little aside.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: The software sounds like a nuisance I can manage, not a threat to the climbing work. My tight budget still bothers me, even in a future where AI barely changes anything.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you cut first if a bill came in before payday?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I’d stop buying coffee on the drive and postpone replacing my work boots if the old pair remained safe. I would not skip the rent or borrow from my sister without first checking my pay.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: You sound sure about the job but less sure about money; how do those sit together?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: They are separate worries for me. I believe the crew still needs my judgment here, but one surprise expense can still knock my budget over.

say: A **job-sheet program** can tidy records, but it cannot judge a line from the road.
A person still checks **site safety** before the crew touches equipment.
think: This small change is unlikely to remove my **outside crew work**.
My **thin budget** worries me more than the software does.
do: Check the **job-sheet details** before using them in a safety briefing.
Keep the call-out rota and **bring lunch from home** to save a little.
feel: I feel **steady about work**, while everyday bills still press on me.
S0.quote: The crew still has to go and look before anyone touches the equipment.
fieldNote: Daria separates **routine records** from the physical inspection that anchors her confidence.
Her calm job outlook does not erase **ongoing budget strain** or the risk of borrowing.

steps.text: Check each generated job sheet before the safety briefing
Bring lunch from home instead of buying it on call-out days
Set aside the small lunch savings after payday

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Steady Disruption: Now picture this. AI brings strong change, but not a revolution. Over the next few years it takes over many thinking tasks in many jobs: writing, checking, planning, buying, booking, coding and answering customers. Robots spread into hands-on work more slowly. Some jobs shrink, new ones appear, and lots of people have to change how they work. Most people still have work, and there is some time to adjust.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I’d say the computer may sort the outage list and order supplies, but it must not send a crew up without a proper site check. If fewer office staff are needed, the company should tell us plainly what happens to our hours.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: The planning part of my lead job could shrink, and then there may be fewer crews sent out. I can still judge the poles and weather today, but I know that does not make my role untouchable.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I’d ask for the company’s written training schedule and learn its new equipment checks with another senior worker beside me. I would keep doing the field job carefully and track my hours, because lower pay would hit my rent quickly.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I’m anxious because the thinking tasks in my role are real, even if the crew work is hands-on. I don’t like new systems arriving before the people responsible for safety have been properly taught.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you tell your crew if the dispatch desk began changing its process?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I’d tell them to check every location and isolation detail with their own eyes before accepting the job. I’d ask my manager to put the training and any change to overtime in writing.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: You want training but prefer familiar methods; what would make you willing to learn the new checks?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I’d learn them if a qualified person showed us on the equipment, instead of sending a link and calling that training. I’d still keep the printed procedure in the truck until I had seen the new method work safely.

say: AI can sort **outage lists**, but it must not skip a site check.
The company should explain any **hours or crew changes** plainly.
think: Planning is part of my lead role and may **shrink**.
Field skill helps, but it does not make my job **untouchable**.
do: Request written **training details** and learn equipment checks with a senior worker.
**Track my paid hours** while continuing the field job carefully.
Keep the **printed procedure** until I have checked the new method.
feel: I feel **anxious** about fewer crews and untested safety changes.
S1.quote: I can still judge the poles and weather today, but I know that does not make my role untouchable.
fieldNote: She acknowledges the exposure of **planning tasks** inside her field-lead role.
Her willingness to adapt depends on **hands-on instruction** and written employment terms from the company.

steps.text: Request written company training on the new equipment checks
Continue leading field inspections and use the printed procedure
Track paid hours and set aside any overtime income

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: AGI by 2028: Next one. The singularity hits fast. Within 2 years, by 2028, there is full AGI: artificial general intelligence, meaning AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do, as well or better, and cheaper. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2031. It arrives before most companies, governments and families have time to prepare.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I’d say the planning, records and fault diagnosis are not jobs people can count on after 2028. We would still have a few years before the robot date, but that is not enough reason to pretend the physical work is secure.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I would be afraid that the company cuts lead positions first and then waits for robots before reducing field crews. I cannot tell whether I would be kept, so I’d want to make a practical plan while I still have wages.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Now I’d ask the company to fund a line-safety instructor course and complete it before 2028 if they agree. In 2029 I’d apply for instructor posts and check the actual duties, because lesson plans and inspections are thinking work too.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: It makes me anxious, but I can do something before then by asking for training and putting aside even a small amount. I would worry if layoffs were announced, but I am not lying awake now as if a loss were certain.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you say to your sister about this short timeline?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I’d tell my sister I may need to stay with her briefly if my wages stop, but I don’t want to plan on her paying my bills. I’d ask her to talk through that possibility before there is an emergency.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Instructor work and inspection still use thinking; could either be protected after full AGI?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: No, I can’t call either one protected after 2028 because AI could make lesson plans and diagnoses too. I’d consider them only as openings that might exist for a while, and I’d keep asking what happens to hands-on crews before 2031.

say: Planning, records and diagnosis are **not protected** after full thinking AGI.
The three-year gap before robots is **time to prepare**, not a guarantee.
think: Lead positions could shrink before the **field crews** do.
I cannot know whether I’d be kept, so I need a **practical plan**.
do: Ask for a company-funded **line-safety instructor course** before 2028.
Apply for **instructor posts** in 2029 and check their actual duties.
Discuss **temporary housing** with my sister without relying on her income.
feel: I feel **anxious**, with actions I can take before a definite loss.
S2.quote: I cannot tell whether I would be kept, so I’d want to make a practical plan while I still have wages.
fieldNote: Daria sees risk in **lead jobs and crews**, without claiming her own loss is certain.
Her response pairs a course with a **family fallback**, though her sister offers no promised rescue.

steps.text: Request company funding for a line-safety instructor course
Apply for instructor openings in 2029 after checking the duties
Talk with my sister about possible short-term housing

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: AGI by 2031: Now the same thing, a bit slower. Full AGI arrives within 5 years, by 2031: AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2034. There are a few years to see it coming, but it's still fast.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I’d say five years is enough to learn the company’s safety changes properly and ask about crew plans before a deadline arrives. I would not say the lineworker job is safe just because robots come later in 2034.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: The later date gives me more time than the 2028 case, and I could finish a course without rushing. Still, AGI could take planning and diagnosis in 2031, and I’d have only three years before the stated robot arrival.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I’d request a training timetable this year and set aside a fixed small amount after each pay. In 2032 I’d apply for safety instructor jobs if there are genuine openings, and keep a copy of the duties before deciding.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I’m still anxious because a five-year warning does not tell me where the next pay cheque comes from. It does make me less rushed than the two-year case, and I can ask questions while the crew is still working.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would make you trust a training place enough to spend your own time on it?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I’d want a supervisor to show the actual qualification and name employers that have hired people with it. I won’t pay for an online promise that the course leads to a permanent safe job.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Would you move to another town for an instructor opening?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Only if the salary and duties were written down and I could afford the move without borrowing. A new town is a serious step when my savings are this thin.

say: Five years allows time to learn **safety changes** and ask about staffing.
The later robot date does not make line work **automatically safe**.
think: I could finish training without the **rush** of a two-year warning.
I still need a real opening and a way to cover **moving costs**.
do: Request a written **training timetable** and save a fixed small amount per pay.
Apply for verified instructor posts in **2032** and review duties.
Move only with **written pay** and enough money for relocation.
feel: I feel **less rushed**, but the next income remains uncertain.
S3.quote: I’m still anxious because a five-year warning does not tell me where the next pay cheque comes from.
fieldNote: She uses extra time to **check training quality**, not assume the qualification has value.
Thin savings make relocation conditional on **written pay** and affordable costs.

steps.text: Request a written timetable for the company’s safety course
Save a fixed small amount after each pay
Apply for verified safety instructor vacancies in 2032

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: AGI by 2036: Last one. Full AGI arrives within 10 years, by 2036: AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2039. It's the same end point, but there's about a decade to prepare, change careers and make plans.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I’d say ten years gives workers time to learn and save, but it is still a real end date for planning work and later physical work. The company should let us know how it will handle changes before 2036 rather than wait until the last minute.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I could put more aside and decide carefully whether to move into training work while I’m still young enough to change direction. The long warning doesn’t solve rent this month, and an instructor job can also be done by thinking AI.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Now I’d take a recognized safety-instructor course one evening at a time and build an emergency fund toward three months of bills. In 2037 I’d apply where duties and wages are clear, and ask how much of the job is still hands-on.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Ten years feels more manageable than two because I can prepare without rushing my family or leaving a job impulsively. It is not secure, though, and today’s low savings still make me careful.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would your partner notice changing this year?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: My partner Sam would see me reserve one evening for the course and stop spending on small things after work. We would keep our current rental until there was a real job offer, rather than move because of a prediction.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Would you treat instructor work as a safe place after full AGI?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: No, lesson planning and diagnosis are thinking work, so I would not call the role safe after 2036. I’d use it as a possibility to check and keep the emergency fund for whichever work is actually available.

say: Ten years gives time to prepare, while planning work changes by **2036**.
The company should explain its **transition plan** before the deadline.
think: I can save and consider a **careful career change**.
Instructor work is also **exposed**, and current bills remain real.
do: Take a recognized **safety-instructor course** one evening at a time.
Build **emergency savings** toward three months of bills.
Apply in **2037** only where pay and duties are clear.
feel: I feel **more prepared than rushed**, but not financially secure.
S4.quote: The long warning doesn’t solve rent this month, and an instructor job can also be done by thinking AI.
fieldNote: A decade changes her **pace of preparation**, but does not ease her current money constraint.
She recognizes that **teaching work** and diagnosis remain exposed after full AGI arrives.

steps.text: Take a recognized evening course in line safety instruction
Build emergency savings toward three months of bills
Apply for clear-pay instructor vacancies in 2037
Keep the current rental with Sam until an actual offer arrives

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Of the five pictures, which one worries you most, and what would actually help you if it happened?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: AGI by 2028 worries me most because it gives little time before thinking work changes and only until 2031 before the robot date. Paid, recognized training during work hours, written information about staffing, and enough pay to save would help me make a sensible choice.

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Is there anything I didn’t ask that I should have?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: Ask whether the people who already know the lines will be included when new systems are tested. I’m not against every tool, but safety is learned with people beside you, not from a notice posted after the change.

headlineQuote: I’m not against every tool, but safety is learned with people beside you, not from a notice posted after the change.
portrait: Daria is a **27-year-old crew lead** who takes pride in careful field judgment.
She has **under one month saved** and few similar local jobs to move into.
She wants **proven instruction** before adopting new systems and relies on family as a fallback.
She sees warning time as useful for **training and saving**, while refusing to call desk or teaching work safe.
biggestWorry: AGI by **2028** leaves little time before thinking tasks change and robots arrive in 2031.
whatWouldHelp: **Paid recognized training**, written staffing information and enough income to build savings would help.
